purpose: Close ASVS V1.3.6, V13.2.4 and V13.2.5 on the two call sites that fetch a destination an outside party chose. The scheme check closed in #4805 proves the URL is of a safe kind and says nothing about where it points; http://127.0.0.1:8200 and http://169.254.169.254 are ordinary http URLs. Destinations are now vetted by address, the connection is pinned to the address that was vetted so a second resolution cannot be substituted, and every redirect hop is vetted again.
requiredInvariants: The guard is on the two untrusted-destination sites and nowhere else, and that is a decision rather than an oversight. Of thirteen outbound fetch sites, eleven take a destination the operator chose - ML_SERVICE_URL, VAULT_ADDR, object storage, the two AI services which already allowlist hosts, and the Telegram and VK constants. Those resolve into private space by design, so a blanket policy would refuse ml-service:8001 and vault:8200 and break working integrations while protecting nothing.

No existing partner integration is broken, and the claim is measured rather than assumed: webhook subscriptions live in an in-memory Map with no Prisma model, so none survives a restart. Even so the default is the public-unicast category rather than a host allowlist, because a partner endpoint is by nature an arbitrary public address and a default-deny host list would make the feature unusable.
Every resolved address is checked, not the first. A name can carry a public A record and a loopback one, and the attacker picks which the connection uses.

The socket connects to the address that was vetted, via the lookup hook. Resolving to check and then handing the name to the client leaves a second resolution between check and connect, and that gap is DNS rebinding.
Every redirect hop is vetted again from the scheme onward, with a bounded hop count. A 302 is a new destination chosen by the same untrusted party.
IPv6 forms carrying an IPv4 address inside are unwrapped and judged on what is inside. ::ffff:127.0.0.1 is loopback in different notation, and 6to4, NAT64 and Teredo embed addresses too.
Octal, hexadecimal and integer spellings are refused rather than reinterpreted. A resolver may read 0177.0.0.1 as loopback; this policy refuses to give the string a second reading.

Fail closed everywhere: an unparseable address, a failed or empty resolution, a redirect without a location, too many redirects and a transport error are all refusals, and a refusal reason is distinguishable from a connection failure so a case cannot pass by failing to connect to something it should have refused.

Paths and default ports are deliberately unconstrained, and the reasoning is written down. A path is the partner's own endpoint; a port restriction on a public address protects nothing once every internal destination is removed by the address rules, while breaking partners on non-standard ports.

Registration business logic beyond this validation, 1C, marketing and presentation are not touched. No production, REG.RU, DNS, database or credential mutation, no migration, no new dependency - the transport is node:http and node:https.
acceptance: ip-address-policy.spec.ts passes 47 of 47 and safe-outbound-request.spec.ts passes 33 of 33; the whole security and partner-api set is 180.

Six mutations are caught: checking only the first resolved address fails 1, re-resolving at connect time fails 1, following a redirect without re-vetting fails 3, dropping the literal-address check fails 2, dropping IPv4 link-local fails 9, dropping the IPv4-mapped IPv6 unwrapping fails 4.

All three verdicts revoke at the matrix level: dropping the every-address loop rejects V1.3.6, dropping the host:port narrowing rejects V13.2.4, and returning the dispatcher to a bare fetch rejects V1.2.2, V1.3.6, V13.2.4 and V13.2.5 together.
The matrix rebuilds at applied 332 / rejected 0, PASS 114 to 117 and FAIL 105 to 102, with no other verdict moved.
tsc --noEmit exit 0, node --test scripts/security passes in full, guard=0.
